semantic_correction.stem: An obstetric emergency team has been activated for a rapidly deteriorating client. Which team practice best supports a safe, coordinated response?

options.A: Assign emergency roles and use standardized communication so assessment, medications, equipment, and escalation proceed with clear accountability.
options.B: Have the most experienced clinician direct each task as it arises, while the rest of the team waits for individual instructions before taking action.
options.C: Let team members choose tasks based on availability and give updates informally, allowing the response to adapt without predefined roles or briefs.
options.D: Confirm the exact obstetric diagnosis first, then assign team roles and use structured communication once the cause of deterioration is established.

semantic_correction.rationale: ACOG guidance on preparing for obstetric and gynecologic emergencies states that emergency protocols should designate team-member roles, that early briefs can assign essential roles and establish expectations, and that standardized communication such as SBAR and closed-loop strategies can support clear information exchange during a time-critical response. ACOG's current Emergencies in Clinical Obstetrics training continues to teach teamwork, communication, and performance of key responsibilities during common obstetric emergencies. Current Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health obstetric-hemorrhage resources also use a designated obstetric rapid-response team and a standardized emergency management plan. Therefore A is correct because it establishes role accountability and structured information exchange from the start. B creates serial task assignment and delays simultaneous team action. C removes the role structure and standardized communication intended to reduce omissions and confusion. D delays organization and communication until after diagnostic certainty even though emergency coordination is needed during the initial response.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Use clearly assigned emergency roles and standardized communication to coordinate simultaneous interprofessional actions during a rapidly evolving obstetric emergency.
semantic_correction.source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Preparing for Clinical Emergencies in Obstetrics and Gynecology; Emergencies in Clinical Obstetrics (ECO)
semantic_correction.source_version_date: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 590, March 2014, live guidance page rechecked August 20, 2026; current ACOG ECO page rechecked August 20, 2026; AIM Obstetric Hemorrhage Patient Safety Bundle revised 2022 and current page rechecked August 20, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 590 — Planning/Rapid Response Team: implement a protocol that designates each team member's role; early response brief assigns essential roles, establishes expectations, and anticipates contingencies; communication protocols such as SBAR, check-back, and call-out support clear or closed-loop communication. Conclusion: inpatient emergencies can be mitigated by a rapid response team with designated roles and streamlined communication. ACOG ECO current course objectives: demonstrate key responsibilities and practice teamwork/communication during obstetric emergencies. AIM Obstetric Hemorrhage Patient Safety Bundle Readiness: designated rapid-response team and standardized facility-wide stage-based emergency management plan.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: A safe obstetric emergency response uses designated team roles and structured communication so multiple urgent actions can be handled efficiently with clear responsibility rather than delayed, improvised without role clarity, or organized only after diagnostic certainty.
semantic_correction.blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
semantic_correction.blueprint_locator: Management of Care, printed p.7 (official PDF pageno 10): prioritize care based on acuity; identify and collaborate with multidisciplinary team members; initiate, evaluate and update the plan of care; recognize limitations and utilize resources; organize workload to manage time effectively. Detailed Management of Care, printed p.21 (official PDF pageno 24): collaboration with multidisciplinary team; Concepts of Management — identify roles and responsibilities of health care team members and plan overall strategies to address client problems.
semantic_correction.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — role clarity, multidisciplinary coordination, and structured emergency response
semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the obstetric emergency-team construct, removed the old all/only distractor cue, rebuilt the alternatives as plausible strategies of nearly identical length, strengthened currentness with live ACOG/AIM resources, and after the first GitHub reread removed the lexical echo of ‘coordinated’ from the correct option.

scope_exclusions.specific_obstetric_diagnosis: The item tests emergency-team coordination rather than management of hemorrhage, eclampsia, shoulder dystocia, cord prolapse, sepsis, or another specific diagnosis.
scope_exclusions.single_leader: A team leader remains important; the key does not reject leadership. It rejects a serial response in which the rest of the team waits for one-by-one instructions instead of functioning within assigned roles.
scope_exclusions.sbar_exclusivity: SBAR is an example of standardized communication, not the only acceptable structured tool; the key intentionally uses the broader term standardized communication.
scope_exclusions.delegation_law: The item does not assign a jurisdiction-specific delegated nursing task or alter scope-of-practice rules.
scope_exclusions.diagnostic_certainty: Emergency organization and communication should not wait for complete diagnostic certainty when the client is already rapidly deteriorating.
scope_exclusions.facility_protocol: Exact role titles and emergency protocols vary by facility; the tested principle is designated roles plus structured communication.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for ‘obstetric emergency designated roles standardized communication SBAR team response’ returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank scan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches ACOG's designated-role and standardized-communication model and establishes clear responsibility for simultaneous emergency actions.
option_audit.B: Plausible because emergency leadership matters, but serially waiting for individual directions underuses assigned team roles and can delay concurrent tasks.
option_audit.C: Plausible because flexibility is necessary in emergencies, but unstructured self-selection and informal updates increase the risk of duplicated or omitted tasks.
option_audit.D: Plausible because diagnosis guides definitive treatment, but role assignment and structured communication are needed during the initial response before diagnostic certainty is complete.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A is the only option combining role clarity with structured communication from the start. B creates serial dependence, C removes structure, and D delays coordination until after diagnostic certainty.
